title: Vision 5: The Shepherd comes to stay
sum: Hermas is at home after prayer when a glorious man dressed as a shepherd sits down beside him and says he has been sent by 'the most revered angel' to live with him for the rest of his life. When the stranger's form changes, Hermas recognizes him as the guardian he had been 'handed over to', and is ashamed of his rude answer. The Shepherd tells him to write first the commandments and the parables, so that he can read them at any time and keep them. Hermas then turns to his readers: keep them and receive what the Lord promised; refuse to repent and receive the opposite.

Lake's heading note: the chapter 'is clearly intended as an introduction to the Mandates, but it is always quoted as the Fifth Vision'. Codex Sinaiticus calls it a 'Revelation'; the Athos manuscript a 'Vision' (see the variant at 25:0).

views.H: The join between the Visions and the Mandates. Hermas speaks as if he already had a guardian, though, as Lake notes, 'there is no mention of this in the preceding Visions' (25:3). The Latin headings ('here begin the twelve commandments of the Shepherd'; 'the beginning of the Shepherd') show that some copies began a new book here, which fits the view that the work grew in stages.
views.N: The Shepherd's gear (staff and bag) is the gear Jesus told the Twelve not to take (Matthew 10:10). An angel who appears as a man and is recognized later recalls Genesis 18 and Judges 13.
views.J: A heavenly guide who explains what the seer saw, and commands him to write, is the pattern of Jewish apocalypses such as 4 Ezra and 1 Enoch, and of Revelation (Revelation 1:11, 19).
views.D: The chapter introduces the book's central figure: an angel put in charge of repentance (25:7). Later chapters say he was given by 'the glorious angel' (78:3), whose identity is debated (see 77 and 89).

echoes: Genesis 18:2; Judges 13:16-22; Tobit 5:4; Matthew 10:10; Revelation 1:11; Revelation 1:19; Psalm 23:1; John 10:11

settings.what: The Shepherd appears and gives his charge
settings.by: The Shepherd, an angel in a shepherd's dress
settings.when: after the four Visions of the old woman and the beast
settings.why: To introduce the guide who will give the commandments and parables, and to tell Hermas to write them first so that they can be read and kept at any time (25:5).
settings.readers: Christians in Rome who would hear the book read: Hermas was told to read it 'in this city with the elders who lead the church' (8:3, Vision 2.4.3).

settings.by: Hermas
settings.when: as the commandments are about to begin
settings.why: To set the terms of the book: keeping the commandments brings what the Lord promised; hearing without repenting brings the opposite.
settings.readers: The Roman church of Hermas's day, many of whom, by the book's own account, had sinned after baptism (31:4).

title: Mandate 1: Believe in one God
sum: The first commandment is a creed in two sentences. Believe that God is one, the Creator who made everything out of what did not exist, who holds all things and is held by nothing. Then fear him, and out of that fear practice self-control. Keeping this throws off wickedness and puts on virtue, and the one who keeps it 'will live to God'.

Irenaeus, about AD 180, quoted 26:1 with the words 'the Scripture declared' (Against Heresies 4.20.2), and Eusebius says Irenaeus 'not only knows, but also receives' the Shepherd (Church History 5.8.7). Faith, fear and self-control return as Mandates 6, 7 and 8 (35:1).

views.H: Irenaeus quotes the verse as Scripture, and Eusebius copies Irenaeus's Greek, so here the Greek of Hermas is known from a writer of the 100s, long before the manuscripts.
views.N: One God (James 2:19; 1 Corinthians 8:6) who made what is out of what is not (Romans 4:17; Hebrews 11:3). Lake's margin adds Ephesians 3:9.
views.J: The creed is Israel's (Deuteronomy 6:4). Creation 'not from things that were' is the teaching of the mother in 2 Maccabees 7:28, which Lake's margin cites.
views.D: A clear early statement of creation from nothing (creatio ex nihilo) and of God's being beyond any place. Hermas names neither the Son nor the Spirit here; his first commandment is about God the Creator.

echoes: Deuteronomy 6:4; James 2:19; 1 Corinthians 8:6; Ephesians 3:9; 2 Maccabees 7:28; Wisdom of Solomon 1:14; Hebrews 11:3; Romans 4:17

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, who is to write it down and hand it on (25:5)
settings.when: the first of the twelve commandments
settings.why: To lay the foundation of everything that follows: faith in the one Creator, fear of him, and self-control.
settings.readers: Believers who had come to faith from the gods of Rome, for whom 'God is one' marked them off from their neighbors; later, Irenaeus's church in Gaul, which read the line as Scripture.

title: Mandate 2: Simplicity, slander and giving
sum: Be simple and innocent, like little children who do not know evil. The commandment then names two tests of simplicity. Do not slander, and do not enjoy listening to slander, because the listener shares the sin. Slander is 'a restless demon'. And give to everyone in need from what God gives you, without sorting out who deserves it. The receivers will answer to God for why they took; the giver who gave simply is innocent, and his giving is a service glorious with God.
Lake notes that the Didache gives the same rule of giving and calls it 'the commandment' (Didache 1:5). Sinaiticus is missing from 27:6 to the end of the commandment (Lake's footnote).

views.H: The commandment and Didache 1:5 share the rule and its reasons (God wants his gifts given to all; the receiver answers for why and for what). Lake points out the parallel; the direction of borrowing is not settled.
views.N: Slander (James 4:11), the innocence of children (Matthew 18:3), and giving to all who ask (Matthew 5:42; Luke 6:30).
views.D: Almsgiving here rests on the giver's 'simplicity', and the moral weight falls on those who receive falsely. The churches' views on almsgiving and merit are on the card at Proverbs 16.
views.R: In a Roman city full of beggars and of clients seeking patrons' gifts, the question 'whom to give to' was a daily one. Hermas tells believers not to act as patrons sorting out the worthy.

echoes: Matthew 18:3; 1 Corinthians 14:20; James 4:11; James 3:8; Didache 1:5; Didache 4:7; Matthew 5:42; Luke 6:30; 2 Corinthians 9:12

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, and through him his household (27:7)
settings.when: the second commandment
settings.why: To make simplicity of heart concrete in two everyday areas, speech and money, so that 'your repentance and the repentance of your household' is real (27:7).
settings.readers: A Roman congregation with rich and poor members, where gossip and the sharing of goods were live issues (compare 14:5 on the rich).

title: Mandate 3: Love the truth
sum: Love the truth and let only truth come out of your mouth, because the spirit God made to live in your flesh is true, and the Lord who lives in you is true. Liars cheat the Lord of the 'deposit' he left with them. Hearing this, Hermas weeps: he has never in his life spoken a true word, and has always passed off lies as truth in business. The Shepherd says his grief is right, and gives him a way forward: speak the truth from now on, and even the old untrue words may become believable.
The scene is one of the book's most personal. Sinaiticus is missing from 28:2 to the last words of the commandment.

views.H: Hermas's confession matches what Vision 1 says of him (a freed slave in business, 1:1) and the book's warnings on business (40:4). Lake finds 28:5 obscure, and suggests Hermas must now make his old promises come true.
views.N: The 'deposit' (2 Timothy 1:14) and grieving the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30) are both echoed. Lake's margin also cites 1 John 2:27 ('true, not a lie').
views.D: Whether 'the spirit God made to live in this flesh' is the Holy Spirit or the human spirit is open (see the note on 28:1). Either way, lying is treated as a wrong done to God, not only to people.
views.R: Business in Rome ran on trust and on talk. A trader who 'passed off lies as truth' and was never contradicted was a familiar figure; Hermas makes him the subject of the commandment.

echoes: Ephesians 4:25; Ephesians 4:30; 2 Timothy 1:14; 1 John 2:27; Colossians 3:9; Luke 19:8

settings.what: The third commandment, with Hermas's confession
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, who weeps over his own lying
settings.when: the third commandment
settings.why: To show that truth-telling is owed to God, and that a liar who repents can begin again from now on (28:5).
settings.readers: Believers in trade and business in Rome, where Hermas himself had worked (28:5; 40:4).

title: Mandate 4.1: Purity, adultery and divorce
sum: The fourth commandment begins with purity of thought: do not let thoughts of another man's wife enter your heart; remember your own wife, and you will not go wrong. Then Hermas asks hard practical questions. If a man finds his believing wife in adultery, may he stay with her? Yes, until he knows; but if she will not repent, he must divorce her and stay single. If she repents, he must take her back, because there is 'one repentance' for God's slaves. The same holds for a husband. And living like the Gentiles is adultery too.

Lake's note: Hermas is working out the clash between Jesus' ban on divorce and the rule not to live with an immoral partner. Separation here is 'not strictly divorce, as the innocent party was not free to remarry'.

views.H: One of the earliest Christian rulings on a real marriage case. Lake reads it against Mark 10:11, Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:11, and notes that Tertullian later accused Hermas of lowering the moral standard (29:11).
views.N: Divorce and remarriage: Matthew 5:32; Matthew 19:9; Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18; 1 Corinthians 7:10-11, all on Lake's margin or in his note. Adultery of thought: Matthew 5:28.
views.D: Hermas forbids remarriage after separating from an adulterous spouse and requires taking back the penitent. The churches' readings of divorce and remarriage today are on the cards at Matthew 5, Matthew 19, 1 Corinthians 7, Deuteronomy 24 and Malachi 2.

echoes: Matthew 5:28; Matthew 5:32; Matthew 19:9; Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18; 1 Corinthians 7:10-11; Hosea 1:2; James 4:4

settings.what: The command to purity of thought
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, whose first sin was a thought about Rhoda (1:2-8)
settings.when: the fourth commandment
settings.why: To guard the heart, where adultery begins, and to point Hermas to his own wife.
settings.readers: Married believers in Rome; the book's opening (1:1-8) shows that its first readers knew Hermas's own story.

settings.by: Hermas asks; the Shepherd answers
settings.when: Hermas asks 'a few things' (29:4)
settings.why: To answer a pastoral case: what a believer must do when a spouse commits adultery, so that the innocent party does not share the sin and the guilty party can still repent.
settings.readers: Roman Christian households facing adultery, divorce and the question of taking a penitent spouse back, as the church at Corinth had faced its own marriage questions (1 Corinthians 7).
views: Lake: the chapter explains 'the practical problem which arose from the conflict between the Christian precept against divorce ... and the equally early precept against having intercourse with immoral persons'.
The case illustrates the rule of 'one repentance' (29:8), which 31 then explains.

title: Mandate 4.2: Repentance is understanding
sum: Hermas confesses that he understands nothing and that his past has hardened his heart. The Shepherd answers with a definition: 'I am in charge of repentance ... and I give understanding to all who repent.' To repent is itself great understanding. The sinner sees what he has done before the Lord, stops doing evil, does good generously, and humbles and punishes his own soul. Hermas asks so many questions, he says, because he is a sinner and needs to know how to live.
Clement of Alexandria repeats the point about AD 200: the Shepherd 'says that repentance is great understanding' (Stromata 2.12-13). Sinaiticus is missing from 30:3 to 31:4.

views.N: The hardened heart of Mark 6:52 (Lake's margin), and the grief that leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10-11). 'Done evil before the Lord' is the verdict of Judges (Judges 2:11).
views.D: Lake saw in Hermas 'the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance'; 30:2, where the penitent humbles and punishes his soul, is one of the verses behind that judgment. The same verse puts the turn to doing good at the center.
views.J: Repentance as returning and humbling the soul draws on the Hebrew Bible (Leviticus 16:29; Psalm 35:13; Joel 2:12).

echoes: Mark 6:52; Judges 2:11; 2 Corinthians 7:10-11; Leviticus 16:29; Joel 2:12; Luke 15:17

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: between the marriage ruling and the question of baptism
settings.why: To show that repentance is a new way of seeing as well as of living, and that the Shepherd gives that understanding.
settings.readers: Readers in Alexandria knew this teaching by about AD 200, when Clement repeated it (Stromata 2.12-13).

title: Mandate 4.3: Is there repentance after baptism?
sum: The book's central question. Hermas has heard 'some teachers' say there is no repentance except the one at baptism, when 'we went down into the water'. The Shepherd agrees in principle: the forgiven should sin no more. But the Lord, who knows human weakness and the devil's schemes, has 'set a repentance' for those already called, and has given the Shepherd authority over it. New believers have baptism's forgiveness. A baptized person who falls has 'one repentance'. One who sins again and again and repents will hardly live.

Here Codex Sinaiticus ends, in the middle of 'he said' (31:6). From here the only continuous Greek is the Athos manuscript of the 1400s, which at the key point reads 'and does not repent'; Lake follows the Latin and Ethiopic, 'and repents' (see the variant).

views.H: Lake: 'The main problem, which constantly recurs, is that of sin after baptism', and in Hermas's circle 'the belief obtained that Christians after baptism were capable of leading sinless lives, and that if they fell they could not again obtain forgiveness'. Hermas's answer was a repentance that 'would not avail more than once'. Lake suggests the 'teachers' had Hebrews 6 in mind.
views.N: Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26 are the New Testament texts nearest to the rigorist teachers. 1 John 1:9 and 1 John 5:16, Jesus' 'seventy-seven times' (Matthew 18:21-22) and the restoring of a sinner at Corinth (2 Corinthians 2:5-11) stand on the other side.
views.D: This chapter is the start of a long history: Clement of Alexandria's 'second repentance', Tertullian's attack on 'the Shepherd of adulterers', the once-only public penance of the early church, and the later sacrament of penance, which the Catholic Catechism calls 'the second plank [of salvation] after the shipwreck which is the loss of grace' (1446). See the deep section.
views.R: The Roman church of Hermas's day had lived through times of pressure in which some had denied the Lord (6:2-8). How to receive back the fallen was a pastoral emergency, not a theory.

echoes: Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 10:26; Hebrews 12:17; 1 John 1:9; 1 John 5:16; Matthew 18:21-22; 2 Corinthians 2:5-11; Acts 2:38

settings.what: The ruling on repentance after baptism
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, who reports what 'some teachers' say
settings.when: after the definition of repentance (30)
settings.why: To answer the teachers who left no hope for baptized sinners: a single further repentance is open, now, to those already called, without making sin easy for new converts.
settings.readers: Baptized Christians in Rome who had fallen into serious sin and were told by some teachers that they could not be restored; Hermas is to preach this repentance to them (46:2-3).
views: The repentance is for 'those who were called before these days' (31:4), like the fixed day of Vision 2 (6:5): an offer to Hermas's generation, not a standing rule.
A standing rule of one repentance
Clement of Alexandria read it as a lasting rule: after baptism God gives 'a second repentance', and repeated repentances are no better than unbelief (Stromata 2.13).

deep.b:
Lake. In his introduction Lake sums up the book's message: 'for sin after baptism there was still the possibility of forgiveness for those who repented, though this repentance would not avail more than once', and he adds that 'we have here the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance'. That is one scholar's judgment, given here as his.

Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200) retells this chapter almost line by line. 'The one who has received forgiveness of sins ought to sin no more' (Stromata 2.13, from the same words as 31:2). God, 'who knows hearts' and foresaw the devil's cunning, gave those who fall even after coming to faith 'a second repentance' (metanoian deuteran), so that one tempted 'after the calling' may receive 'one more repentance'. Then Clement quotes Hebrews 10:26-27 and warns that 'continual and successive repentances' are no different from never having believed. So Clement read Hermas and Hebrews together: one further repentance, not a habit.

Tertullian (about AD 210-220), by then a Montanist, attacked the bishop who readmitted adulterers. He dismissed the Shepherd as 'the scripture of the Shepherd, which alone loves adulterers' (scriptura Pastoris, quae sola moechos amat, On Modesty 10.12), and said the Epistle of Barnabas, which he took to be the letter to the Hebrews, was 'more received among the churches than that apocryphal Shepherd of adulterers' (20.2). Tertullian's complaint shows that some churches of his day appealed to Hermas for the readmission of serious sinners.

Later practice. The Catholic Catechism describes the early centuries: Christians who had committed grave sins after baptism had to do public penance, often for years, before being reconciled, and in some regions admission to the order of penitents was 'only once in a lifetime'. From the seventh century a private form spread from Ireland that 'envisioned the possibility of repetition' (Catechism 1447). The Catechism calls the sacrament of Penance 'the second plank [of salvation] after the shipwreck which is the loss of grace' (1446). So the Catholic practice the Catechism describes no longer keeps Hermas's limit of one repentance. How the churches differ on whether a believer can fall and be restored is on the card at Hebrews 6, and on confession to a priest on the card at Psalm 32.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the 'one repentance' as a door held open, not a ration
deep.b: Read beside 29:8, the 'one repentance' looks less like a limit on God's mercy than a pastoral guard against a church becoming a revolving door. In 29 the same phrase explains why a husband must take back a penitent wife 'but not over and over': the marriage, like the church, can absorb one great failure and a true return, but not endless betrayal without change. In 43:4 the double-minded 'are always repenting' and go to fortune-tellers. On this reading Hermas is fighting two errors at once: the teachers who allowed no return (31:1), and believers who treated repentance as a routine (31:6). The 'one' then names the seriousness of repentance more than an arithmetic of forgiveness. This is my reading; it overlaps with Clement of Alexandria's warning against 'continual and successive repentances', but Clement still keeps the count at one.

title: Mandate 4.4: Marrying again after a death
sum: Hermas asks one more marriage question: if a husband or wife dies and the survivor marries, is that a sin? No, says the Shepherd, though one who stays single gains 'more honor and great glory with the Lord'. He ends the fourth commandment with a charge to guard purity and reverence, and a promise: from the day Hermas was handed over to him, the Shepherd will live in his house, and those who keep the commandments will have their earlier sins forgiven.
Lake's margin points to 1 Corinthians 7:38-40, which the Shepherd's answer follows closely.

views.N: Paul allows a widow to remarry 'only in the Lord' and judges her 'more blessed if she stays as she is' (1 Corinthians 7:39-40; compare Romans 7:2-3; 1 Timothy 5:14).
views.D: Hermas permits a second marriage after a death and praises staying single, a balance the churches have kept in different ways. The cards at 1 Timothy 3 (married, celibate and remarried clergy) and Judith 16 (lifelong widowhood) take up the questions.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 7:38-40; Romans 7:2-3; 1 Timothy 5:14; 1 Timothy 3:2

settings.what: The question of a second marriage, and the close of the fourth commandment
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: after the ruling on repentance (31)
settings.why: To settle a marriage question that troubled believers, and to end the commandment on purity with assurance of forgiveness for the obedient.
settings.readers: Widows and widowers in the Roman church, whose care the book entrusts to Grapte (8:3).

title: Mandate 5.1: Patience and bad temper
sum: The fifth commandment sets patience against bad temper. In a patient person the Holy Spirit lives in a roomy place and serves God with cheerfulness. When bad temper moves in, the delicate Spirit feels cramped, is choked, and tries to leave, because the Lord lives in patience and the devil in bad temper. Two spirits cannot share one house. A drop of wormwood spoils a whole jar of honey; so bad temper spoils patience, even its prayer. The Shepherd promises to be with all who repent with their whole heart.
In 33:5 the Athos manuscript is garbled, and Lake prints a text the editors rebuilt from the Latin, the Ethiopic and Antiochus (see the variant).

views.N: Patience as the Spirit's fruit (Galatians 5:22), anger that does not do God's righteousness (James 1:19-20), and the Spirit living in the believer (1 Corinthians 3:16).
views.D: Hermas pictures the Holy Spirit as a guest who can be crowded out and leave. The line 'all of them were justified by the most revered angel' (33:7) is one of the puzzles of his teaching about Christ and the angels (see the note).
views.J: Two spirits contending in one person is a picture Hermas develops in Mandate 6 (36), where two angels are with each human being.

echoes: Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29; Galatians 5:22; James 1:19-20; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 4:30; Deuteronomy 29:18

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, who asks how bad temper works (33:7)
settings.when: the fifth commandment
settings.why: To show bad temper as a spiritual danger, not a small fault: it drives out the Holy Spirit and spoils prayer.
settings.readers: Households and a congregation in which quarrels over 'everyday matters' were common (34:2), and in which Hermas's own household needed the warning (33:7).

title: Mandate 5.2: How bad temper works
sum: The Shepherd now explains how bad temper works. It cannot touch those full of faith, but it slips into the empty and double-minded and makes them bitter over nothing: food, a small thing, a friend, a gift or a debt. Patience is great and strong, cheerful and calm. Bad temper starts as foolishness and grows into bitterness, rage, anger and lasting fury, and ends in a sin that cannot be healed. When these spirits move in, the Holy Spirit leaves, and the empty person is filled with evil spirits and blinded. If Hermas masters this commandment, he can keep the rest.
The family tree of anger (34:4) shares three words with Ephesians 4:31.

views.N: Ephesians 4:31 lists 'bitterness, rage and anger'; the house left empty and filled by worse spirits recalls Matthew 12:43-45.
views.D: Hermas says that the Spirit can leave a person and evil spirits take his place (34:6-7). The question of whether a believer can fall away is on the card at Hebrews 6.
views.R: Quarrels over food, small things, friends, gifts and debts (34:2) are the everyday business of a Roman household and its network of friends and clients.

echoes: Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8; Matthew 12:43-45; Matthew 6:24; James 1:8

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: continuing the fifth commandment
settings.why: To trace bad temper from its small beginnings to its end, so that the hearer stops it early, and to call this the key to keeping all the commandments (34:8).
settings.readers: Believers whose quarrels over money, food and friends the book knows well (34:2); the 'empty and double-minded' were among them (34:1).

title: Mandate 6.1: The straight road and the crooked
sum: The sixth commandment picks up the first: faith, fear and self-control each have powers that 'go two ways', toward what is righteous and toward what is unrighteous. Trust what is righteous, the Shepherd says. Its road is straight and level, without thorns or stumbling blocks. The crooked road has no real paths, only rough and thorny ground. Hermas would like to walk the straight road, and the Shepherd says he will, and so will anyone who turns to the Lord with his whole heart.

views.N: The narrow and the wide road (Matthew 7:13-14).
views.J: The straight and crooked paths of Proverbs (Proverbs 2:13-15) and the way of the righteous and the wicked in Psalm 1:6 stand behind Hermas's two roads. The Didache and Barnabas open their own Two Ways with 'There are two ways' (Didache 1:1; Epistle of Barnabas 18:1).
views.H: Hermas's form of the Two Ways is short and tied to his scheme of faith, fear and self-control; it is not the long list of the Didache. The two angels of 36 make it his own.

echoes: Psalm 1:6; Proverbs 2:13-15; Jeremiah 21:8; Matthew 7:13-14; Didache 1:1; Epistle of Barnabas 18:1; Jeremiah 24:7; Joel 2:12

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the sixth commandment, looking back to the first (35:1)
settings.why: To show that every virtue has a direction, and to invite Hermas to choose the straight road.
settings.readers: Christians who knew the Two Ways teaching from their instruction, as the Didache and Barnabas show it was taught.

title: Mandate 6.2: The two angels
sum: Two angels are with every human being, one of righteousness and one of wickedness. How can Hermas tell them apart? By their works in the heart. The angel of righteousness is delicate, modest, gentle and quiet, and talks of righteousness, purity, reverence and contentment. The angel of wickedness is bad-tempered and bitter, and brings desires for business, feasts, drink, luxury, women, greed and pride. Even a faithful man who lets the bad angel's thought stay will sin, and even a wicked man moved by the good angel will do some good. So follow the one, and say goodbye to the other.

views.J: The nearest picture on the site is Barnabas's Two Ways, with angels of God over the way of light and angels of Satan over the way of darkness (Epistle of Barnabas 18:1). Hermas brings the two angels inside each person.
views.N: 'You will know who they are from their fruit' (Matthew 7:16); Lake's margin cites it at 36:4. The good angel's virtues and the bad angel's works are close to the Spirit's fruit and the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:19-23).
views.D: Hermas adds an angel of wickedness beside the good one. The cards at Matthew 18:10, Psalm 91 and Tobit 5 give how the churches answer whether everyone has a guardian angel.
views.R: The bad angel's list (business, lavish meals, drinking, luxury, women, greed, boasting) reads like the life of a prosperous household in Rome.

echoes: Matthew 18:10; Psalm 91:11; Acts 12:15; Epistle of Barnabas 18:1; Matthew 7:16; Galatians 5:19-23; James 3:13-18

settings.what: The two angels and how to know them
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, who asks how to tell the two angels apart (36:2, 36:5)
settings.when: the second half of the sixth commandment
settings.why: To give Hermas a practical test: watch what rises in your heart, and you will know which angel is speaking.
settings.readers: Believers living among the temptations of a wealthy city (36:5); the commandment speaks of 'man or woman' (36:7-8), so it was meant for both.

title: Mandate 7: Fear the Lord, not the devil
sum: Fear the Lord and keep his commandments, and you will be strong in everything. But do not fear the devil, because he has no power over those who fear the Lord; people fear only what has power. Fear the devil's works instead, and keep away from them. So there are two kinds of fear: the fear of the Lord keeps you from doing evil and moves you to do good. Asked why he said 'they will live to God', the Shepherd explains: all creation fears the Lord, but only those who also keep his commandments have life with God.

views.N: 'Fear God and keep his commands' (Ecclesiastes 12:13), which Lake's margin cites; 'Stand up against the devil' (James 4:7); fear God, not those who can kill only the body (Matthew 10:28).
views.J: The fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom and the root of obedience runs through the Hebrew Bible (Proverbs 1:7; Deuteronomy 10:12).
views.D: The commandment explains Hermas's refrain 'you will live to God' (37:5): fear alone is not enough; life belongs to those who fear and obey.

echoes: Ecclesiastes 12:13; Proverbs 1:7; Deuteronomy 10:12; James 4:7; Matthew 10:28; 1 Peter 5:8-9

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, who asks about the phrase 'they will live to God' (37:5)
settings.when: the seventh commandment, the second of the three named in 26:2
settings.why: To free believers from fear of the devil by teaching the right fear, of the Lord.
settings.readers: Christians who, by the book's own account, were frightened of the devil's power (48:1) and needed to hear that he has none over them.

title: Mandate 8: What to hold back from, and what not
sum: Self-control, like everything God made, goes two ways. Hold back from evil; never hold back from good. The Shepherd lists the evils to avoid: adultery, drunkenness, luxury, showy wealth, pride, lying, slander, hypocrisy, grudges, then stealing, cheating, false witness, greed, deceit and vanity. Then the goods not to hold back from: faith, the fear of the Lord, love, harmony, truth and endurance, and after them the works of mercy: serving widows, caring for orphans and the needy, ransoming God's slaves, hospitality, respect for the old, bearing insults, encouraging the weak, bringing back those who stumble, and not squeezing debtors.

views.N: James's 'visit orphans and widows' (James 1:27), the works of Matthew 25:35-36, hospitality (Hebrews 13:2), and restoring the fallen (Galatians 6:1).
views.D: Hermas defines self-control as a matter of good and evil, not of food or marriage (compare 1 Timothy 4:3).
views.R: The list shows a Roman church at work: widows, orphans, the poor, travelers to be housed, believers to be bought out of slavery, debt or prison (1 Clement 55:2 tells of Romans who sold themselves to ransom others).

echoes: James 1:27; Matthew 25:35-36; Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2-3; Galatians 6:1; 1 Clement 55:2; 1 Timothy 4:3

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the eighth commandment, the third of the three named in 26:2
settings.why: To turn self-control from a list of refusals into a pattern of life: refuse evil, and give yourself fully to good.
settings.readers: A congregation with widows, orphans, poor members and members who were slaves or in debt (38:10), whom the better-off were to serve.

title: Mandate 9: Do not be double-minded
sum: Do not be double-minded about asking God for things, and do not tell yourself, 'How can I ask the Lord for something and receive it, when I have sinned against him so much?' God is not like people who hold grudges. Turn to him with your whole heart and ask without hesitating, and you will receive. The double-minded get nothing; those complete in faith receive. If an answer comes slowly, it is because of some testing or a sin you do not know about, so keep asking. Double-mindedness is a daughter of the devil, an earthly spirit without power. Faith comes from above, from the Lord, and has great power.

views.N: The chapter reads like an expansion of James 1:5-8 (ask in faith, without wavering; the double-minded man receives nothing), with James 3:15 behind 'earthly' (39:11). Lake's margin cites James 1:8.
views.D: Hermas's double-minded person is above all the sinner who doubts that God will hear him. His cure is not a stronger feeling but turning to the Lord 'with your whole heart' (39:2).
views.H: The shared word dipsychos is one of the strongest links between Hermas and James; whether Hermas knew the letter or both drew on a common way of teaching is argued.

echoes: James 1:5-8; James 4:8; James 3:15; James 1:17; Mark 11:23-24; Luke 18:1-8; Jeremiah 31:34

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the ninth commandment
settings.why: To give sinners confidence to pray: God holds no grudge, so the one who has sinned may still ask and receive.
settings.readers: Believers who, like Hermas, felt their sins made prayer useless (39:1), the 'double-minded' whom the book addresses again and again.

title: Mandate 10.1: Grief, sister of doubt and temper
sum: Put away grief, says the Shepherd, because it is a sister of double-mindedness and bad temper. Hermas cannot see how; the three seem different. Grief, the Shepherd says, is more evil than all the spirits, ruins a person, and wears out the Holy Spirit, and yet it also saves. Hermas does not understand. Those who believe but never seek the truth, and are tangled up in business, wealth and pagan friendships, are like neglected vineyards gone wild with thorns. Those who fear God and seek him understand quickly, because where the Lord lives, there is understanding.

views.N: Grief that brings repentance and grief that brings death (2 Corinthians 7:10); the thorns that choke the word, 'the worries of the age and the trickery of wealth' (Matthew 13:22).
views.R: Business, wealth and 'friendships with Gentiles' (40:4) were the ties of Roman city life, with their meals and religious rites; Hermas treats them as a danger to understanding.
views.J: Lake's margin cites Psalm 111:10 and Proverbs 1:7 (the fear of the LORD and understanding) and Sirach 2:3 (holding fast to the Lord).

echoes: 2 Corinthians 7:10; Matthew 13:7; Matthew 13:22; Proverbs 24:30-31; Isaiah 5:1-6; Psalm 111:10; Proverbs 1:7; Sirach 2:3

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the tenth commandment
settings.why: To show why grief is dangerous, and why only those who seek the Lord can understand his parables.
settings.readers: Believers whose faith had grown dry under business and social ties (40:4), a group the book singles out in the Roman church (14:5).

title: Mandate 10.2: How grief crushes the Spirit
sum: The Shepherd explains. When a double-minded person fails at something, grief comes in and grieves the Holy Spirit. When a person loses his temper and then regrets it, grief comes in too, and this grief seems to bring salvation, because he repents. But both grieve the Spirit: doubt because it failed, temper because it did evil. So put away grief and do not crush the Holy Spirit who lives in you, or he may plead with God and leave. The Spirit of God given to this flesh does not put up with grief or being cramped.
Crombie's English (in the Ante-Nicene Fathers) makes 41 and 42 one chapter; Lake divides them.

views.N: 'Do not cause grief to the Holy Spirit of God' (Ephesians 4:30) and 'Do not snuff out the Spirit' (1 Thessalonians 5:19); Lake's margin cites Ephesians 4:30 at 41:4.
views.D: Hermas speaks of the Spirit as one who can be crushed and can leave. Whether he means the Holy Spirit as a person or as God's power living in us is a question his language leaves open (see 59 on the Spirit in the flesh).
views.H: In 41:5 the witnesses differ ('plead with God', 'plead against you'); Lake follows the versions and explains the sense as asking God to let the Spirit depart.

echoes: Ephesians 4:30; 1 Thessalonians 5:19; Psalm 51:11; Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 6:19; 2 Corinthians 7:10

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the second section of the tenth commandment
settings.why: To explain the riddle of 40:2: grief can lead to repentance, but as a state of mind it crushes the Spirit, so it must be put away.
settings.readers: Believers prone to discouragement after failure or after outbursts of temper, the double-minded and bad-tempered of Mandates 5 and 9.

title: Mandate 10.3: Put on cheerfulness
sum: Put on cheerfulness, which always pleases God, and delight in it. The cheerful do good and think good; the grieving always do evil, because they grieve the Holy Spirit, who was given to people cheerful, and because they neither pray nor confess to the Lord. The prayer of a grieving man cannot rise to God's altar, because grief mixed with prayer is like vinegar mixed with wine. Clean yourself of evil grief, and you will live to God.

views.N: 'God loves a glad giver' (2 Corinthians 9:7); joy as fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22); prayers rising to the altar before God (Revelation 8:3-4).
views.D: Hermas makes joy a duty and grief a sin, which sits uneasily beside the Bible's laments and Jesus' blessing on those who mourn (Matthew 5:4). His 'grief' is the sullen gloom of the double-minded, not sorrow for sin (41:3-4).
views.R: Vinegar and wine mixed in one jar spoil each other. Hermas often draws his pictures from the cellar and the kitchen (33:5; 43:15; 48:3).

echoes: 2 Corinthians 9:7; Galatians 5:22; Philippians 4:4; Revelation 8:3-4; Psalm 141:2; Matthew 5:4

settings.what: The end of the tenth commandment
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the last section of the tenth commandment
settings.why: To replace grief with cheerfulness as the setting in which prayer can rise to God.
settings.readers: A church whose prayer life Hermas describes from the inside, with its sense of prayer rising to God's altar.

title: Mandate 11: The true prophet and the false
sum: The Shepherd shows Hermas people on a bench and a man in a chair: a false prophet, who ruins the double-minded. They come to him like pagans to a fortune-teller, and he answers to suit their desires, empty answers for empty people, with some true words that the devil supplies. How can one tell a true prophet? By his life. The true prophet is gentle, humble and content with little; he does not answer questions or speak in private; he speaks when God wills, in the gathering at prayer, filled with the Holy Spirit. The false one seeks the seat of honor, lives in luxury, takes pay, avoids the righteous, prophesies in corners, and falls silent in a praying church. Small things from above, hail and drops, have power; earthly spirits have none.
Clement of Alexandria quotes 43:3 as the words of 'the Shepherd, the angel of repentance' (Stromata 1.17.85).

views.H: The chapter is a window on a Roman church in which prophets still spoke in the assembly, and some sat in a 'chair' as paid advisers. Lake notes that the 'bench' is the learner's and the 'chair' the teacher's (43:1).
views.N: Testing prophets by their fruit (Matthew 7:15-20) and testing the spirits (1 John 4:1). The Didache gives similar tests: a prophet who asks for money is false (Didache 11:12).
views.D: Hermas assumes true prophecy continues in the church. Whether gifts of prophecy continue today is on the cards at Numbers 11, 1 Corinthians 13, 1 Thessalonians 5 and Romans 12.
views.R: Diviners and paid oracles were part of Roman life (compare Acts 16:16). Hermas calls consulting a false prophet idol worship (43:4).

echoes: Matthew 7:15-20; 1 John 4:1; Didache 11:8; Didache 11:12; Matthew 23:2; Matthew 23:6; Acts 16:16; 2 Peter 1:21; 1 Corinthians 14:29-32; James 3:15

settings.by: The Shepherd, who shows Hermas a scene and explains it
settings.when: the eleventh commandment, given as a scene and a parable (43:18)
settings.why: To teach the church to tell true prophets from false by their lives, not by their claims, and to keep the double-minded from consulting prophets like oracles.
settings.readers: A Roman congregation that met for prayer and heard prophets speak in its gathering (43:9), and some of whose members went privately to a paid prophet (43:2, 43:13).

title: Mandate 12.1: Evil desire and good desire
sum: The twelfth commandment sets two desires against each other. Put away every evil desire and put on the desire that is good and reverent; then you will hate evil desire and rein it in like a horse. Evil desire is wild and hard to tame, and it eats people up, above all God's slaves who have no understanding and are tangled up in this age. It hands them over to death. Hermas asks what its works are, so he can keep away from them.

views.N: The flesh's desire against the Spirit's (Galatians 5:16-17), and James on bridling the body and tongue (James 3:2; James 1:26).
views.D: Hermas speaks of a good desire as well as an evil one, so desire as such is not evil; what matters is what it is set on.

echoes: Galatians 5:16-17; James 1:14-15; James 3:2; James 1:26; Romans 7:7

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the last of the twelve commandments
settings.why: To name the root of many sins and to set against it a stronger, good desire.
settings.readers: God's slaves 'tangled up in this age' (44:2), as the book describes many in the Roman church.

title: Mandate 12.2: The works of evil desire
sum: Above all, evil desire is desire for another's spouse, for showy wealth, for many empty foods and drink, and for foolish luxuries. It is the devil's daughter, and it kills God's slaves. Those mastered by it die in the end. But put on the desire for righteousness, arm yourself with the fear of the Lord, and stand against evil desire, and it will run away and never be seen again, because it fears your weapons. Then, crowned as victor, bring your prize to the desire for righteousness and serve it, and you will master evil desire.

views.N: The armor of God (Ephesians 6:13) and 'Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you' (James 4:7), both on Lake's margin.
views.R: The victor's crown and prize come from the games that Rome loved (1 Corinthians 9:25); Hermas turns the athlete into the servant of righteousness.
views.D: The fear of the Lord is the believer's armor here, as faith is in Ephesians 6:16.

echoes: Ephesians 6:13; Ephesians 6:16; James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:9; 1 Corinthians 9:25; 2 Timothy 4:8; Revelation 4:10

settings.what: The works of evil desire and the victory over it
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: continuing the twelfth commandment
settings.why: To show that evil desire can be beaten, and that the winner's prize belongs to the desire for righteousness.
settings.readers: Believers among the wealth and pleasures of Rome (45:1), for whom 'luxury' was a daily temptation.

title: Mandate 12.3: Can the commandments be kept?
sum: How does one serve good desire? By doing righteousness, virtue, truth, the fear of the Lord, faith and gentleness. With that the twelve commandments are finished. The Shepherd tells Hermas to walk in them and urge his hearers to make their repentance pure for the rest of their lives; he will give Hermas favor and persuade them. But Hermas objects: the commandments are great and good, but too hard for a human being to keep. The Shepherd answers that if Hermas sets it in his mind that they can be kept, he will keep them easily; if he decides they cannot, he will not, and he and his household will not be saved.
Lake: in some copies the Similitudes began here; the Athos manuscript writes 'beginning' at this point and the Ethiopic 'the beginning of the similitudes'.

views.N: 'This command ... is not too strange or hard for you' (Deuteronomy 30:11); 'his commands are not heavy' (1 John 5:3); 'my yoke is kind to wear' (Matthew 11:30).
views.D: The Shepherd's answer seems to rest on resolve alone, but 47:3 and 49:4 add that it is the Lord in the heart, and the Lord's strength, that make the commandments possible. How grace and human will work together is one of the long debates of the church; Hermas speaks pastorally, not as a theologian of grace.
views.H: The notes in A and E (46:3) suggest that the book was once divided differently, with the Similitudes beginning after the twelfth commandment.

echoes: Deuteronomy 30:11; 1 John 5:3; Matthew 11:30; Philippians 4:13; Psalm 19:8

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.when: the end of the twelfth commandment
settings.why: To name the good works that are the service of good desire.
settings.readers: Hearers who would be urged, through Hermas, to make their repentance pure (46:2).

settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, who is given a 'task of service' (46:3)
settings.when: when the twelve commandments are complete
settings.why: To send Hermas to preach repentance with the commandments, and to meet the despair that says they cannot be kept.
settings.readers: The Roman church to which Hermas carried the commandments (46:2-3; 8:3), and in particular those 'who are going to repent' (46:3).

title: Mandate 12.4: Lord of creation, lord of the commandments
sum: The Shepherd's anger at Hermas's doubt is so great that his form changes, and Hermas is terrified. Then he speaks more gently. God made the world for humankind and gave them authority over everything under heaven. If a human being rules God's creatures, can he not rule these commandments? Whoever has the Lord in his heart can. For those who have the Lord only on their lips, they are hard. So put the Lord into your heart; turn back from the devil's commandments; do not fear the devil, for the angel of repentance is with you and masters him.

views.N: Humankind set over creation (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8:6, on Lake's margin), and the people who honor God with their lips while their heart is far (Matthew 15:8; Isaiah 29:13).
views.H: The Athos manuscript adds here a short prayer listing God's works; Lake calls it 'apparently a pious comment inserted in the text by mistake' and leaves it out (see the note on 47:2).
views.D: The answer to 'Can the commandments be kept?' is christological in practice though not in name: 'a person who has the Lord in his heart' can master them (47:3).

echoes: Genesis 1:28; Psalm 8:6; Hebrews 2:6-8; Matthew 15:8; Isaiah 29:13; James 4:7

settings.what: The Shepherd's answer to Hermas's despair
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, and then 'you who are empty and flighty in the faith' (47:5)
settings.when: after Hermas says the commandments are too hard (46:4)
settings.why: To shake Hermas out of despair with anger and then encouragement, and to call the hearers to put the Lord into their hearts.
settings.readers: Hearers addressed directly in the plural (47:5-6), some of whom were walking 'in the devil's commandments'.

title: Mandate 12.5: The devil tests the empty jars
sum: Hermas says people want to keep the commandments and pray for strength, but the devil is hard and overpowers them. The Shepherd answers that the devil cannot overpower those who hope in the Lord with their whole heart. He can wrestle with them but not throw them; resist him, and he runs away in shame. Only the empty fear him. A man with a cellar full of wine checks only the partly empty jars, because they go sour. So the devil tests everyone, but finds a way in only to those whose faith is not full, and they become his slaves.

views.N: 'Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you' (James 4:7, on Lake's margin) and the wrestling of Ephesians 6:12.
views.R: The wine cellar is a scene from Roman life: full jars keep, partly empty ones turn to vinegar.
views.D: Hermas gives the devil real power to test but none to conquer the faithful (1 Corinthians 10:13).

echoes: James 4:7; Ephesians 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8-9; 1 Corinthians 10:13; 43:15

settings.what: Hermas's fear of the devil answered
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance (25:7), speaking to Hermas
settings.to: Hermas, speaking for people who want to obey (48:1)
settings.when: after the Shepherd's call not to fear the devil (47:7)
settings.why: To explain why some believers fall to the devil and others do not: fullness of faith.
settings.readers: Believers who prayed for strength and still felt overpowered (48:1), addressed in the plural (48:2).

title: Mandate 12.6: The angel of repentance speaks to all
sum: The Shepherd speaks in his own name: 'I, the angel of repentance, say to you: do not fear the devil.' He was sent to be with all who repent with their whole heart. Those who have given up on their lives because of their sins should trust God: if they turn to the Lord and serve him rightly for the rest of their days, he will heal their earlier sins, and they will master the devil's works. The devil's threat is as limp as a dead man's sinews. Hermas answers that he is now made strong, and hopes, with the Lord's help, to keep the commandments. The Shepherd ends: all who clean their hearts of empty desires will keep them and live to God.

views.N: 'The one who has power to save and to destroy' (James 4:12, on Lake's margin); fear the One who can destroy soul and body (Matthew 10:28).
views.D: The Mandates end not with a threat but with healing for 'earlier sins' (49:2), and with Hermas's hope that the Lord will make him strong (49:4).
views.H: The closing address to 'you who have given up on your life' (49:2) shows the book's purpose: to reach Christians in despair over sins after baptism, the problem Lake calls 'the main problem, which constantly recurs'.

echoes: James 4:7; James 4:12; Matthew 10:28; Jeremiah 24:7; Joel 2:12; Philippians 4:13

settings.what: The angel of repentance to the despairing
settings.by: The Shepherd, naming himself 'the angel of repentance'
settings.to: All who repent with their whole heart, and those who 'have given up on your life' (49:2)
settings.when: at the close of the twelve commandments
settings.why: To give hope to believers who think their sins have put them beyond help, and to free them from fear of the devil.
settings.readers: Roman Christians who had sinned after baptism and given up hope, the very people the second repentance of 31 was for.

settings.what: Hermas's answer and the Shepherd's last word
settings.by: Hermas, then the Shepherd
settings.to: The Shepherd; then all who clean their hearts
settings.when: the end of the Mandates
settings.why: To end the commandments with confidence that they can be kept with the Lord's strength.
settings.readers: The same hearers, now told that keeping the commandments is possible for all 'who clean their hearts' (49:5).
